quests.instruction: Which idiom best captures this: "The coding test was so simple for her that she finished it in ten minutes, barely thinking."
quests.hint: Like 'piece of cake,' this means something is easy — but it emphasizes how pleasant and effortless it felt, not just how little effort it took.
quests.explanation: 'A walk in the park' means something is very easy, often with a hint that it was also pleasant or stress-free. "For an experienced hiker, that trail is a walk in the park."
quests.origin: A literal comparison to a relaxed, leisurely stroll — effortless compared to more strenuous activity.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The math problem took him three seconds; it was nothing at all, hardly worth mentioning."
quests.hint: Both mean 'easy,' but one idiom focuses purely on how little effort or skill was needed, without implying anything about how pleasant it was.
quests.explanation: 'Piece of cake' fits best here since the sentence is only about how little effort the task took, not about it being enjoyable. Both idioms mean 'easy,' but 'a walk in the park' more often implies a pleasant experience too. "That interview was a piece of cake."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'piece of cake.' This question checks the learner's ability to tell apart two idioms with nearly the same core meaning.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Something extremely easy, often said dismissively about a task others find hard.
quests.explanation: 'Child's play' means something is so easy it could be done by a child. "Compared to the final exam, the quiz was child's play."
quests.origin: A literal comparison to the simplicity of games children play, in figurative use since at least the 1600s.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The flight was delayed six hours with no compensation offered, so she just accepted it and waited it out without complaining."
quests.hint: This idiom is about enduring an ongoing, unpleasant situation with patience, not about making a bold decision.
quests.explanation: 'Grin and bear it' means to endure something unpleasant patiently, without complaining. "There's no fixing the noisy construction next door — we just have to grin and bear it."
quests.origin: A straightforward pairing of a forced smile ('grin') with quiet endurance ('bear it'), recorded in English since the 1800s.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "He hated calling to cancel the contract, but he finally forced himself to make the call and get it over with."
quests.hint: One idiom is about a single decisive act of enduring something difficult right now; the other is about patiently tolerating something ongoing.
quests.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' fits a single decisive act of forcing yourself through something unpleasant, while 'grin and bear it' fits patiently enduring an ongoing situation. "I'll just bite the bullet and make the call now."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'bite the bullet.' This question distinguishes a one-time decisive act from long-term patient endurance.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "Even though the hike was much harder than expected and everyone was exhausted, the group kept pushing through to the summit."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Persist through a difficult situation with determination, rather than quitting.
quests.explanation: 'Tough it out' means to endure a hard situation through sheer determination. "The team had no substitutes left, so they had to tough it out for the final ten minutes."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent use of 'tough' as an adjective turned into an action — being tough through something difficult.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "She'd already signed the lease, but lying awake that night, she started wondering if moving to a new city was really the right call."
quests.hint: This is about reconsidering a decision after the fact, which is different from feeling sudden nervousness right before acting.
quests.explanation: 'Have second thoughts' means to begin doubting a decision you've already made. "I'm having second thoughts about the color we picked for the kitchen."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase: your 'first thought' was the original decision, and a 'second thought' reconsiders it.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Standing at the edge of the diving platform, he suddenly panicked and couldn't make himself jump."
quests.hint: One idiom is about sudden nervousness right at the moment of acting; the other is about doubting a decision over time.
quests.explanation: 'Get cold feet' fits sudden, in-the-moment nervousness right before doing something, while 'have second thoughts' fits doubts that build up over time. "He got cold feet right before walking on stage."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'get cold feet.' This question distinguishes momentary panic from gradual reconsideration.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Withdraw from a plan or agreement you had previously committed to.
quests.explanation: 'Back out' means to withdraw from a commitment. "He backed out of the trip at the last minute."
quests.origin: A literal image of physically retreating backward out of a space or situation, applied figuratively to commitments.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "With no savings and barely enough for rent and food each week, the family had no financial cushion at all."
quests.hint: This describes severe, constant financial struggle — stronger than simply having just enough.
quests.explanation: 'Live hand to mouth' means to live in a state of severe poverty, with barely enough to survive day to day. "After losing his job, he was living hand to mouth for months."
quests.origin: A literal image of food going directly from hand to mouth with nothing stored for later — an image of having no reserves at all.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "They manage okay on two modest salaries, though there's rarely much left over after the bills are paid."
quests.hint: One idiom describes genuine, severe poverty with no reserves at all; the other simply means having just enough to cover expenses.
quests.explanation: 'Make ends meet' fits managing to cover expenses, even if tightly, while 'live hand to mouth' describes more severe, constant financial struggle. "They make ends meet, but there's no room for extras."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'make ends meet.' This question distinguishes it from the more extreme idiom 'live hand to mouth.'

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Spending more money than you actually earn, usually through debt.
quests.explanation: 'Living beyond your means' means spending more than your income allows. "Between the new car and the vacations, they were clearly living beyond their means."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase using 'means' in its older sense of financial resources or income.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "At dinner, she couldn't help herself and told everyone about the surprise party, completely forgetting it was supposed to be a secret."
quests.hint: Both idioms in this pair mean revealing a secret, but one more often implies the reveal was a careless slip rather than deliberate gossip.
options: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG
quests.explanation: 'Spill the beans' can describe either an intentional or accidental reveal of a secret, often through excited talking. "She spilled the beans about the engagement before they announced it."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'spill the beans.' Its origin is disputed — an old theory links it to Greek voting, but it isn't well supported by evidence.

quests.word: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG
quests.instruction: Which idiom more specifically fits a secret getting out purely by accident, almost as a slip of the tongue?
quests.hint: Think about which idiom's traditional image (an animal escaping unexpectedly from a bag) suggests something happening unintentionally.
options: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG
quests.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' leans slightly more toward an accidental, unintentional reveal, while 'spill the beans' can go either way and often implies eager talking. "Oops — I think I just let the cat out of the bag about the surprise."
quests.correctAnswer: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'let the cat out of the bag,' possibly linked to old market scams involving substituted animals, though the precise history is debated.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Accidentally reveal someone's true identity or secret plan.
options: LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG
quests.explanation: 'Blow someone's cover' means to expose their disguised identity or hidden role. "The photo on social media blew his cover as an anonymous reviewer."
quests.origin: From spy and espionage terminology, where a 'cover' is a false identity, and 'blowing' it means exposing the truth.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Ever since the disagreement, she's been curt and distant with him, barely making eye contact."
quests.hint: This idiom describes a milder, more passive form of ignoring someone compared to a more complete, deliberate refusal to interact.
quests.explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' means to act distant and unfriendly toward someone, without full silence. "He's been giving me the cold shoulder since I forgot his birthday."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'the cold shoulder' — possibly from an old custom of serving unwelcome guests a cold cut of meat.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "After the fight, she refused to say a single word to him for three full days."
quests.hint: One idiom involves complete, total silence as a form of punishment; the other is milder — just acting distant and unfriendly, not full silence.
quests.explanation: 'The silent treatment' fits complete, deliberate silence used to punish someone, which is more extreme than the milder distance of 'the cold shoulder.' "He gave her the silent treatment for a week after the argument."
quests.origin: A transparent, modern phrase describing total silence used as a deliberate social punishment.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately exclude someone from a group or conversation.
quests.explanation: 'Freeze someone out' means to deliberately exclude them from a group or activity. "After the disagreement, the rest of the team froze him out of planning decisions."
quests.origin: Related to 'cold shoulder' and 'ice out' — all part of a temperature-based family of idioms for social exclusion.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Before launching, the whole team confirmed they all understood the plan and the timeline the same way."
quests.hint: This idiom is about shared understanding of facts or plans, which is a slightly different focus from sharing the same opinion or values.
quests.explanation: 'On the same page' means everyone shares the same understanding of a situation or plan. "Let's confirm we're all on the same page before the client call."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'on the same page' — a straightforward metaphor from reading the same section of a document together.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The two co-founders have completely different values about how fast to grow the business, and they rarely agree on strategy."
quests.hint: One idiom is about sharing opinions or values, which is the focus here since it's about ongoing disagreement rather than a shared factual plan.
quests.explanation: The sentence describes an ongoing disagreement in opinions and values, which fits 'see eye to eye' (usually used in the negative here) better than 'on the same page,' which is more about shared factual understanding. "They just don't see eye to eye on company culture."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'see eye to eye.' This question distinguishes shared opinion from shared factual understanding.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Reach a compromise where both sides give up part of what they originally wanted.
quests.explanation: 'Meet in the middle' means to compromise, with each side moving partway toward the other's position. "They couldn't agree on the price, so they met in the middle."
quests.origin: A literal spatial image of two people walking toward each other and meeting halfway.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "At the start of the workshop, the facilitator had everyone share an embarrassing childhood story to loosen up the room."
quests.hint: This is specifically about easing initial, first-meeting awkwardness — not about resolving an existing conflict.
quests.explanation: 'Break the ice' means to ease tension in an early, unfamiliar social situation. "The team-building game really broke the ice on the first day."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'break the ice' — from ships called icebreakers that cut a path through frozen water.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The roommates finally sat down and talked honestly about the tension that had been building for weeks over chores."
quests.hint: One idiom is about easing first-meeting awkwardness between strangers; the other is about resolving existing, built-up tension between people who already know each other.
quests.explanation: 'Clear the air' fits resolving existing tension through honest conversation, while 'break the ice' fits easing awkwardness when people are just meeting. "We finally cleared the air about the chore schedule."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'clear the air.' This question distinguishes it from the similar-sounding first-meeting idiom 'break the ice.'

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Gradually start to like or feel comfortable with someone, over time.
quests.explanation: 'Warm up to someone' means to gradually develop positive feelings toward them. "The dog was shy at first but slowly warmed up to the new neighbor."
quests.origin: A literal temperature metaphor, part of the same family as 'break the ice' and 'the cold shoulder,' using warmth for friendliness.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "She saw two coworkers whispering and immediately assumed they were talking about her, without any real evidence."
quests.hint: This is about forming a judgment too quickly, without considering other explanations.
quests.explanation: 'Jump to conclusions' means to form a judgment before having enough information. "Don't jump to conclusions — maybe they were planning your birthday."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'jump to conclusions' — a visual metaphor for skipping the reasoning process entirely.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "He was convinced the new intern had leaked the report, but it turned out to be someone from a completely different department."
quests.hint: One idiom is specifically about accusing or suspecting the wrong person or cause; the other is more general, about deciding too fast without enough information.
quests.explanation: 'Bark up the wrong tree' fits a specific mistaken accusation about who or what caused something, while 'jump to conclusions' is the broader idiom for deciding too quickly in general. "If you think I broke it, you're barking up the wrong tree."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'bark up the wrong tree' — from hunting dogs barking at the wrong tree after losing track of their prey.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Form negative opinions of people or situations too hastily.
quests.explanation: 'Be quick to judge' means to criticize or form opinions about someone too fast, often unfairly. "Try not to be so quick to judge — you don't know her whole situation."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase describing hasty moral evaluation, distinct from the more specific 'jump to conclusions,' which covers any hasty judgment, not just critical ones.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The feedback on her report was about the formatting, but she reacted as if it were a criticism of her intelligence."
quests.hint: This is about misreading a neutral or general comment as a direct attack on yourself.
quests.explanation: 'Take something personally' means to interpret a general or neutral comment as a direct insult. "He didn't mean it as an attack — try not to take it personally."
quests.origin: A transparent phrase treating criticism as either general ('impersonal') or specifically aimed at you ('personal').

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Something about his overly formal tone just irritates her, even though she can't explain exactly why."
quests.hint: One idiom is about someone unintentionally causing irritation in another person; the other is about how a person reacts to something said to them.
quests.explanation: 'Rub someone the wrong way' fits an unintentional source of irritation, while 'take something personally' is about misreading a comment as a personal attack. "His tone rubs a lot of clients the wrong way."
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'rub someone the wrong way' — from stroking fur against its natural direction.

quests.word: HAVE A CHIP ON YOUR SHOULDER
quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Carry ongoing resentment or defensiveness, often from a past grievance, that colors how you react to things.
options: HAVE A CHIP ON YOUR SHOULDER
quests.explanation: 'Have a chip on your shoulder' means to carry constant resentment or a defensive attitude, often stemming from a past slight. "Ever since he was passed over for the promotion, he's had a chip on his shoulder."
quests.correctAnswer: HAVE A CHIP ON YOUR SHOULDER
quests.origin: Believed to come from a 19th-century American custom where a person would balance a wood chip on their shoulder, daring anyone to knock it off and start a fight.
